title: Applied Causal Analysis
text:
Overview
In this note we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the permutation test in the one-sample inference problem when we want to carry out inference for the mean of a random variable. We will consider sign changes as the group transformation and study the behavior of the permutation test and its relationship to the normal approximation when the sample size grows to infinity. We will pay particular attention to what happens when the randomization hypothesis fails.

title: Applied Causal Analysis
text:
0.1 The Central Question
In Chapter 4 we construct a permutation test for the one-sample hypothesis
\[H_0 : \mathbb{E}[W] = 0\]
using sign changes as the group of transformations. Recall that the randomization hypothesis is the key condition that guarantees finite-sample exactness of the permutation test. It will require that the distribution of \(W\) to be symmetric about zero. When the DGP is skewed, this condition fails, and the permutation test is no longer exact. It remains, however, asymptotically valid if we modify the test statistic as we showed in class.
This raises a natural question: if both the sign-change permutation test and the standard normal approximation are only asymptotically valid under a skewed DGP, how do their finite-sample null distributions compare? Chapter 5 answers this question by simulating both distributions under a re-centred exponential DGP, which satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[W] = 0\) but is right-skewed.






ImportantKey Message



The sign-change permutation test is exact if and only if the distribution of \(W\) is symmetric about zero. Under a skewed DGP, both the permutation test and the normal approximation are only asymptotically valid. The permutation test is not a free lunch: its finite-sample guarantees rest on the randomization hypothesis, which is a substantive assumption about the DGP.

text:
3.1 Environment


Load libraries and function library
rm(list = ls())

library(ggplot2)

source("../../programs/ACA_Function_Library.r")

set.seed(42, kind = "L'Ecuyer-CMRG")








Note



The seed is fixed with the L’Ecuyer-CMRG generator, which is safe for parallel execution and ensures reproducibility across sessions.

title: 2  Setup
text:
3.2 The One-Sample Testing Problem
Let \(W^{(n)} = (W_1, \ldots, W_n)\) be an i.i.d. sample drawn from an unknown distribution \(P\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). We wish to test
\[H_0 : \mathbb{E}[W] = 0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_1 : \mathbb{E}[W] \neq 0.\]
This is a one-sample location problem: under \(H_0\) the distribution of \(W\) is centred at zero, but we make no further parametric assumption about its shape.

title: 2  Setup
text:
3.3 The Studentised Test Statistic
A natural test statistic is the studentised mean
\[T_n = T_n\!\left(W^{(n)}\right)
      = \frac{\bar{W}_n}{\hat{\sigma}_n / \sqrt{n}},
\qquad
\bar{W}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n W_i,
\quad
\hat{\sigma}_n^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (W_i - \bar{W}_n)^2.\]
Studentising removes the dependence on the unknown variance and ensures that \(T_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) under \(H_0\) by the central limit theorem, regardless of the shape of \(P\), provided \(\mathbb{E}[W^2]
< \infty\).


Define the studentised test statistic
Tn <- function(data, sample_size, studentized = FALSE) {
  if (studentized) return(mean(data) / sqrt(var(data) / sample_size))
  return(sqrt(sample_size) * mean(data))
}








Note



The function Tn() accepts a logical argument studentized. When studentized = TRUE it returns \(\bar{W}_n / (\hat{\sigma}_n/\sqrt{n})\); when FALSE it returns the non-studentised version \(\sqrt{n}\,\bar{W}_n\). All subsequent analyses use the studentised form.

title: 2  Setup
text:
3.4 The Data-Generating Process
We generate \(n = 1000\) observations from the re-centred exponential distribution:
\[W_i = \text{Exp}(1) - 1, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n.\]
This DGP satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[W_i] = 0\), so \(H_0\) is true by construction. However, \(W_i\) has skewness \(+2\), which means it is not symmetric about zero. The asymmetry will be important when we discuss the randomization hypothesis in Chapter 4.


Generate data from the re-centred exponential
n   <- 1000
B   <- 499
alpha <- 0.05

W_n     <- rexp(n, rate = 1) - 1
Tn_obs  <- Tn(W_n, n, studentized = TRUE)

cat("Sample size n       :", n,     "\n")


Sample size n       : 1000 


Generate data from the re-centred exponential
cat("Monte Carlo draws B :", B,     "\n")


Monte Carlo draws B : 499 


Generate data from the re-centred exponential
cat("Significance level  :", alpha, "\n")


Significance level  : 0.05 


Generate data from the re-centred exponential
cat("Observed T_n        :", round(Tn_obs, 4), "\n")


Observed T_n        : 0.254 




Plot the sample distribution
df_w <- data.frame(W = W_n)

ggplot(df_w, aes(x = W)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    x     = expression(W[i]),
    y     = "Density",
    title = expression("Re-centred exponential: " * W[i] == Exp(1) - 1)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 3.1: Histogram of the re-centred exponential sample \(W_i = \text{Exp}(1) - 1\). The distribution is right-skewed; its mean is zero but it is not symmetric about zero.





The red dashed line marks zero. The distribution is clearly right-skewed: most mass lies close to zero but there is a long right tail, so the distribution is not symmetric about its mean.

title: 3  The Sign-Change Permutation Test
text: 4 The Sign-Change Permutation Test

title: 3  The Sign-Change Permutation Test
text:
4.1 The Sign-Change Group
In the two-sample problem of the previous notes, the group \(\mathbf{G}_n\) consisted of all permutations of the treatment vector. For the one-sample problem, the natural group is instead the set of all sign changes.






ImportantDefinition: Sign-Change Group



Let \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = (\epsilon_1, \ldots, \epsilon_n) \in
\{-1, +1\}^n\). The sign-change group is
\[\mathbf{G}_n = \left\{ g_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} : g_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
W^{(n)} = (\epsilon_1 W_1, \ldots, \epsilon_n W_n) \right\},\]
with cardinality \(M = \#\mathbf{G}_n = 2^n\).


Each element of \(\mathbf{G}_n\) flips the sign of a subset of observations while leaving their absolute values unchanged. Since \(M = 2^n\) grows exponentially in \(n\), exact enumeration is infeasible even for moderate sample sizes; we therefore draw \(B\) elements of \(\mathbf{G}_n\) uniformly at random.

title: 3  The Sign-Change Permutation Test
text:
4.2 The Randomization Hypothesis
Recall the general framework from the previous notes. The permutation test is finite-sample exact at level \(\alpha\) if the law \(P_n\) satisfies the randomization hypothesis with respect to \(\mathbf{G}_n\):
\[W^{(n)} \stackrel{d}{=} g_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\, W^{(n)}
\quad \forall\, g_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \in \mathbf{G}_n,
\quad \text{whenever } P_n \in \Omega_0.\]
For the sign-change group, this condition requires that the joint distribution of \((W_1, \ldots, W_n)\) is invariant under arbitrary sign flips of its coordinates. Under i.i.d. sampling, this reduces to the requirement that the marginal distribution of each \(W_i\) be symmetric about zero:
\[W_i \stackrel{d}{=} -W_i.\]






WarningThe Randomization Hypothesis Fails Here



The re-centred exponential \(W_i = \text{Exp}(1) - 1\) has \(\mathbb{E}[W_i] = 0\) but is right-skewed (skewness \(= +2\)). It is not symmetric about zero, so
\[W_i \stackrel{d}{\neq} -W_i,\]
and the randomization hypothesis does not hold. The sign-change permutation test is therefore not exact for this DGP. Both the permutation test and the normal approximation are only asymptotically valid. Their finite-sample behaviour is compared in Chapter 5.


The precise relationship between the null hypothesis and the randomization hypothesis is worth stating explicitly:








Condition
Randomization hyp. holds?
Test is exact?




\(P\) symmetric about 0
Yes
Yes


\(P\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[W]=0\), asymmetric
No
No (asymptotic only)

title: 3  The Sign-Change Permutation Test
text:
4.3 Applying the Sign-Change Group
The function group.action() from the function library implements the Monte Carlo approximation: it draws \(B\) elements of \(\mathbf{G}_n\) uniformly at random and returns an \(n \times B\) matrix whose \(b\)-th column is \(g_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(b)}} W^{(n)}\).


Apply B random sign changes to W_n
W_n_perm <- group.action(W_n, B, type = "sign.changes")

# W_n_perm is an n x B matrix; column b is the b-th sign-changed sample
dim(W_n_perm)


[1] 1000  499

title: 3  The Sign-Change Permutation Test
text:
4.4 Recomputing \(T_n\) Over Sign Changes
For each column \(b = 1, \ldots, B\) we recompute the studentised statistic on the sign-changed data:


Compute permuted test statistics
Tn_perm <- apply(W_n_perm, 2, function(x) Tn(x, n, studentized = TRUE))


The collection \(\{T_n(g_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(b)}} W^{(n)})\}_{b=1}^{B}\) approximates the randomization distribution of \(T_n\) under \(\mathbf{G}_n\).

title: 3  The Sign-Change Permutation Test
text:
4.5 The Permutation Critical Value
Fix \(\alpha \in (0,1)\). Stack the \(B\) permuted statistics with the observed statistic and sort them:
\[T_n^{(1)}(w) \leq T_n^{(2)}(w) \leq \cdots \leq T_n^{(B+1)}(w).\]
Define \(k = (B+1) - \lfloor (B+1)\alpha \rfloor\). The permutation critical value is
\[\hat{c}_n(1-\alpha) = T_n^{(k)}(w).\]


Compute the permutation critical value
Tn_all <- c(Tn_perm, Tn_obs)
k      <- length(Tn_all) - floor(length(Tn_all) * alpha)
cv_perm <- sort(Tn_all)[k]

cat("Permutation critical value:", round(cv_perm, 4), "\n")


Permutation critical value: 1.7509 


Compute the permutation critical value
cat("Normal critical value z_{1-alpha}:", round(qnorm(1 - alpha), 4), "\n")


Normal critical value z_{1-alpha}: 1.6449

title: 3  The Sign-Change Permutation Test
text:
4.6 The Permutation Test Decision
The one-sided permutation test rejects \(H_0\) whenever the observed statistic exceeds the permutation critical value:
\[\phi_n^{\text{perm}} = \mathbf{1}\left\{ T_n > \hat{c}_n(1-\alpha) \right\}.\]


Apply the permutation test
result <- perm_test(Tn_all, alpha)
cat("Reject H0 (1 = yes, 0 = no):", result, "\n")


Reject H0 (1 = yes, 0 = no): 0

title: 3  The Sign-Change Permutation Test
text:
4.7 The Permutation P-Value
An equivalent summary is the permutation p-value
\[\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B+1} \sum_{b=1}^{B+1}
\mathbf{1}\!\left\{ T_n^{(b)}(w) \geq T_n(w) \right\},\]
where the sum includes the observed statistic itself as the \((B+1)\)-th element.


Compute the permutation p-value
p_perm <- mean(Tn_all >= Tn_obs)
cat("Permutation p-value:", round(p_perm, 4), "\n")


Permutation p-value: 0.422

title: 4  Finite-Sample Comparison
text: 5 Finite-Sample Comparison

title: 4  Finite-Sample Comparison
text:
5.1 Two Asymptotically Valid Procedures
As established in Chapter 4, neither the sign-change permutation test nor the normal approximation is exact for the re-centred exponential DGP, because the randomization hypothesis fails. Both procedures are, however, asymptotically valid under \(H_0 : \mathbb{E}[W] = 0\), in the sense that
\[\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_{H_0}\!\left[\phi_n^{\text{perm}} = 1\right] = \alpha,
\qquad
\lim_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{P}_{H_0}\!\left[\phi_n^{\text{asy}} = 1\right] = \alpha,\]
where \(\phi_n^{\text{asy}} = \mathbf{1}\{T_n > z_{1-\alpha}\}\) and \(z_{1-\alpha} = \Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)\) is the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).
The question is: how do the two procedures compare in finite samples? We answer this by simulating the randomization distribution (via sign changes applied to the observed \(W^{(n)}\)) and the asymptotic null distribution (by drawing fresh samples from \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), which is what \(T_n\) converges to under \(H_0\)), and comparing both to the \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) reference.

title: 4  Finite-Sample Comparison
text:
5.2 Simulating the Asymptotic Null Distribution
Under \(H_0\), the CLT guarantees \(T_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). We approximate this limiting distribution by drawing \(B\) independent samples of size \(n\) from \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) directly and computing \(T_n\) on each:


Simulate the asymptotic null distribution
simulated_asymtest <- numeric(B)

for (i in seq_len(B)) {
  W_asym             <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  simulated_asymtest[i] <- Tn(W_asym, n, studentized = TRUE)
}

Tn_all_asym <- c(simulated_asymtest, Tn_obs)








Note



Drawing from \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) rather than from the true DGP (the re-centred exponential) is deliberate: the \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) samples represent the limiting distribution that \(T_n\) converges to, i.e. the distribution the normal approximation implicitly assumes. Comparing the randomization distribution against this reference directly shows how well the normal approximation characterises the finite-sample behaviour of \(T_n\).

title: 4  Finite-Sample Comparison
text:
5.3 Critical Values


Collect the two critical values
cat("Permutation critical value  cv_perm :", round(cv_perm, 4), "\n")


Permutation critical value  cv_perm : 1.7509 


Collect the two critical values
cat("Normal critical value  z_{1-alpha}  :", round(cv_asym, 4), "\n")


Normal critical value  z_{1-alpha}  : 1.6449 


Collect the two critical values
cat("Difference (cv_perm - cv_asym)      :", round(cv_perm - cv_asym, 4), "\n")


Difference (cv_perm - cv_asym)      : 0.106 


A positive difference indicates that the permutation test uses a more conservative critical value than the normal approximation; a negative difference indicates the opposite.

title: 4  Finite-Sample Comparison
text:
5.4 Visualising the Two Null Distributions


Plot the two null distributions
# Combine into a tidy data frame for ggplot
df_perm <- data.frame(Tn = Tn_perm,          dist = "Randomization")
df_asym <- data.frame(Tn = simulated_asymtest, dist = "Asymptotic (N(0,1))")
df_all  <- rbind(df_perm, df_asym)

ggplot(df_all, aes(x = Tn, fill = dist)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 bins = 50, alpha = 0.45,
                 position = "identity", colour = "white") +
  stat_function(fun  = dnorm,
                args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1),
                colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cv_perm, colour = "steelblue",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cv_asym, colour = "red",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Randomization" = "steelblue", "Asymptotic (N(0,1))" = "grey60")
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = cv_perm + 0.06, y = Inf, vjust = 2,
           label = paste0("Perm. c.v. = ", round(cv_perm, 3)),
           colour = "steelblue", size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = cv_asym + 0.06, y = Inf, vjust = 4,
           label = paste0("z_{1-a} = ", round(cv_asym, 3)),
           colour = "red", size = 3.2, hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    x    = expression(T[n]),
    y    = "Density",
    fill = NULL,
    title = "Randomization vs. Asymptotic Null Distribution"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The blue dashed line marks the permutation critical value \(\hat{c}_n(1-\alpha)\) and the red dashed line marks the normal critical value \(z_{1-\alpha}\).

title: 4  Finite-Sample Comparison
text:
5.5 Interpreting the Comparison
Several features of the plot deserve attention.
Shape of the randomization distribution. The randomization distribution is obtained by applying sign changes to the observed sample \(W^{(n)}\). Because the re-centred exponential is right-skewed, the observed sample itself is skewed, and this skewness is inherited by the randomization distribution. The distribution therefore does not centre exactly on zero and may deviate from the \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) reference in the tails.
Shape of the asymptotic distribution. The simulated asymptotic distribution is generated by drawing fresh \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) samples and computing \(T_n\) on each. Because these samples are symmetric, the resulting distribution of \(T_n\) closely tracks the \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) reference, as expected.
Discrepancy between the critical values. When the two critical values differ, the two tests will reach different rejection decisions for the same observed \(T_n\). This discrepancy reflects the finite-sample cost of using the sign-change permutation test under a DGP for which the randomization hypothesis fails.






TipTakeaway



When the randomization hypothesis holds (symmetric DGP), the sign-change permutation test is exact and the normal approximation is only asymptotically valid — the permutation test strictly dominates. When the randomization hypothesis fails (skewed DGP), both tests are asymptotically valid, and the comparison reduces to a finite-sample question about which critical value is closer to the true \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of the null distribution of \(T_n\). There is no theoretical guarantee that the permutation test is better in this case.

title: 4  Finite-Sample Comparison
text:
5.6 Exactness Under the Randomization Hypothesis
For completeness, we restate the exactness theorem from the previous notes in the current context.






TipTheorem (Finite-Sample Exactness)



If \(P_n \in \Omega_0\) satisfies the randomization hypothesis with respect to \(\mathbf{G}_n\), then
\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\phi_n^{\text{perm}}\!\left(W^{(n)}\right)\right] = \alpha
\quad \text{for all } P_n \in \Omega_0.\]


Under the re-centred exponential, the precondition of this theorem — the randomization hypothesis — does not hold. Exactness is therefore not guaranteed, and the result above does not apply.
